```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(purrr)
library(broom)
```

## Problem 1
```{r}
set.seed(2026)

birthday_repeated <- function(n) {
  n_val <- n[[1]]
  birthdays <- sample(1:365, size = n_val, replace = TRUE)
  
  length(unique(birthdays)) < n_val
}

birthday_results_df <- expand_grid(
  number_of_people = 2:50,
  iter = 1:10000
) |> 
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(number_of_people, birthday_repeated)
  )

birthday_summary_df <- birthday_results_df |> 
  group_by(number_of_people) |> 
  summarize(prob_of_repeat = mean(repeated), .groups = "drop")

birthday_plot <- birthday_summary_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = number_of_people, y = prob_of_repeat)) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 23, linetype = "dashed", color = "#d95f02") +
  geom_line(color = "#2b5c8f", linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_point(color = "#2b5c8f", size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Birthday Problem Simulation (10,000 Runs per Group Size)",
    subtitle = "Probability that at least two people share a birthday in a group of size n",
    x = "Group Size (Number of People)",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

print(birthday_plot)
```

Problem 1 comment: 
The plot itself shows steep, nonlinear trend upwards and confirms the birthday paradox that the probability that at elast 2 people share a birthday rises steeply and non-linearly with group size, crossing 50% at just about 23-25 people and about 100% by 50 people. 


## Problem 2

**Step 1: Create Tidy Dataframe:**
```{r df}

# 1. Start with a dataframe containing all file names
study_df <- tibble(
  file_path = list.files(path = "./data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
) %>%
  mutate(file_name = basename(file_path))

# 2. Iterate over file names, parse metadata, and read data using purrr::map
tidy_study_data <- study_df %>%
  mutate(
    parsed = str_match(file_name, "^([a-z]+)_([0-9]+)\\.csv$"),
    arm = parsed[, 2],
    subject_id = parsed[, 3]
  ) %>%
  select(-parsed) %>%
  mutate(
    data = map(file_path, ~ read_csv(.x, show_col_types = FALSE))
  ) %>%
  unnest(data) %>%
  
  # 3. Tidy the result: pivot weekly observations from wide to long format
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    week = str_remove(week, "week_") %>% as.integer()
  ) %>%
  select(subject_id, arm, week, observation, file_name)

print(tidy_study_data)
```
**Step 2: Spaghetti Plot**
```{r plot}
# Create the spaghetti plot
spaghetti_plot <- tidy_study_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = subject_id, color = arm)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, labeller = labeller(arm = c(con = "Control Arm", exp = "Experimental Arm"))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("con" = "#2b5c8f", "exp" = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(
    title = "Participant Trajectories Over Time by Study Arm",
    subtitle = "Individual subject observations across 8 weeks",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation Value",
    color = "Study Arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "none", 
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

print(spaghetti_plot)

ggsave("spaghetti_plot.png", plot = spaghetti_plot, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```
Spaghetti Plot observations over time: 
From the two plots, we can see that while the subjects in the control arm followed a somewhat static trend where there were local increases and decreases in y-values between week to week, the y-values largely end where they started across the 8 weeks. 
Meanwhile there is a general trend upwards (or positive trend) for the experimental arm across the 8 weeks. While there were local decreases in the y-value from week to week for individuals, the general trend is one that increases. 

## Problem 3
**Step 1: t-testing**
```{r ttest}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(2026)

# 1. Define a helper function for a single simulation iteration
sim_ttest <- function(n = 30, mu = 0, sigma = 5) {
  sim_data <- rnorm(n = n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  
  t.test(sim_data, mu = 0) %>%
    tidy() %>%
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)
}

# 2. Run 5,000 simulations for each true mu in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
sim_results <- expand_grid(
  true_mu = 0:6,
  iter = 1:5000
) %>%
  mutate(
    test_res = map(true_mu, ~ sim_ttest(n = 30, mu = .x, sigma = 5))
  ) %>%
  unnest(test_res) %>%
  mutate(
    rejected = p_value < 0.05
  )

print(sim_results)
```
**Step 2: Plots**
```{r plot3}
# Plot 1: 
power_plot <- sim_results %>%
  group_by(true_mu) %>%
  summarize(power = mean(rejected), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2b5c8f", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2b5c8f", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power vs. True Effect Size (μ)",
    subtitle = "One-sample t-test (n = 30, σ = 5, α = 0.05, 5,000 simulations per μ)",
    x = "True Value of μ",
    y = "Power (Proportion Rejected)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

print(power_plot)

ggsave("power_plot.png", plot = power_plot, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)

# Plot 2
estimate_summary <- bind_rows(
  sim_results %>%
    group_by(true_mu) %>%
    summarize(mean_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(sample_group = "All Samples"),
  sim_results %>%
    filter(rejected) %>%
    group_by(true_mu) %>%
    summarize(mean_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(sample_group = "Rejected Nulls Only (p < 0.05)")
)

estimate_plot <- estimate_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = mean_mu_hat, color = sample_group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "All Samples" = "#2b5c8f",
      "Rejected Nulls Only (p < 0.05)" = "#d95f02"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimate (μ̂) vs. True Value of μ",
    subtitle = "Comparing all simulated datasets against subsets where H₀ was rejected",
    x = "True Value of μ",
    y = "Average Estimate of μ̂",
    color = "Dataset Subset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

print(estimate_plot)

ggsave("estimate_plot.png", plot = estimate_plot, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```
Plot descriptions for Problem 3: 

1. Describe the association between effect size and power: 

We see that as effect size increases, power (proportion of times the null was rejected) also increases. However, at about effect size of 3, power rises to close to 100% and stays there under the current set population size, variance, and alpha. 

2. Is the sample average of μ hat across tests for which the null is rejected approximately equal to the true value of μ? Why or why not?

Not across al values of μ. As shown by the orange "Rejected Nulls Only" curve, the sample average of μ(hat) among rejected tests is inflated above the true value of μ for small positive effect sizes (μ = 1,2,3) and only converges back to true μ when μ = 0 or when μ >= 4. 

This occurs because of selection bias. When statsitical power islow, conditioning on p < 0.05 filters out estimates close to zero and retains only extreme upper-tail samples where random positive noise pushed μ(hat) past the critical t-value. By contrast, at μ = 0 positive and negative false-positive rejections cancel out symmetrically around zero, while at high effect sizes (μ >= 4) near-100% power ensures almost all datasets reject the null without tuncation.
